title: How to Calculate Capital Gains on NPS Tier II Withdrawals
description: NPS Tier II is an optional, flexible investment account with no lock-in period, unlike Tier I. Contributions to NPS Tier II are not eligible for tax deduction.

faq.q: Is NPS Tier II mandatory for all NPS subscribers?
faq.a: No, NPS Tier II is completely optional. It is a voluntary savings account that can be opened by any existing Tier I subscriber.

faq.q: Are contributions to NPS Tier II tax-deductible?
faq.a: Generally, no. Contributions to NPS Tier II do not qualify for tax deductions under Section 80C or 80CCD, unlike Tier I contributions.

faq.q: How is long-term capital gain calculated for NPS Tier II debt investments?
faq.a: For debt investments held for more than 36 months, long-term capital gains are calculated by subtracting the indexed cost of acquisition from the sale proceeds. The indexed cost adjusts the purchase price for inflation using the Cost Inflation Index (CII).

faq.q: Can I choose my asset allocation in Tier II?
faq.a: Yes, similar to Tier I, you have the option of 'Active Choice' where you can decide the percentage allocation across equity, corporate debt, government securities, and alternative assets, or 'Auto Choice' where allocation is age-dependent.

faq.q: What is the main difference between Tier I and Tier II taxation?
faq.a: Tier I offers tax benefits on contributions and is largely tax-exempt on withdrawal (up to 60% lump sum, balance for annuity). Tier II contributions are not tax-deductible, and withdrawals are subject to capital gains tax on the profits made.

faq.q: Do I need to pay tax if I re-invest the withdrawn amount from Tier II?
faq.a: The act of withdrawal itself triggers capital gains tax on the profits realised. Re-investing the amount elsewhere does not exempt you from paying tax on the gains from the original withdrawal.

faq.q: What if I have multiple partial withdrawals from my NPS Tier II account?
faq.a: Each partial withdrawal is treated as a separate redemption event. You must calculate the capital gains for each withdrawal individually, using the FIFO method to determine the cost of acquisition for the units redeemed.
